doc.title: Adrian Cunningham interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 31, 2021

title: Learning on the gig and Wycliffe Gordon's example
summary: Ninety percent is learned on the gig, including professionalism, and he credits Wycliffe Gordon, in whose quintet he plays, as a human and musical influence.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Are there other things that you learned, like on the bandstand or from older musicians that you had not learned in music school?

Oh yes. I would say ninety percent of it. Ninety percent of what you learn is on the gig you know. From the obvious things, and this is such a cliché, turning up on time, looking good, answering emails or texts when they come in about gigs and not just leaving — you know, all of those obvious things are something that is kind of misplaced I think with young kids coming up, and I was probably like that too as a youngster, a little bit complacent about calling back or being really professional. And I think that’s something that you can only learn doing the gig or losing the gig and asking yourself why didn’t I get called again? That’s an important lesson. But I think beyond that, and a huge, probably the most important thing about me being in New York is what you learn from the energy of a master when you’re next to them onstage. And I think hearing the masters of course is priceless. But being next to — I mean Wycliffe Gordon is one of my biggest influences just in terms of a human being, beyond the music. I’ve been in his quintet for, what, six or seven years now, and just to be next to that man and to feel his energy and to see how he handles situations dealing with musicians, dealing with the business, dealing with having a bad day and being up on stage. That sort of education is priceless, I don’t even know how to put it into words. It’s the presence of someone like that.
